1.	Hold on in Korea until the Chinese communists either surrender or until the French and VietNamese have smashed the communist rebels in Indo-China, the British have crushed them in Malaya and the Filipinos have eliminated them from their islands. These are not impossible.
2.	Settle the Kashmir dispute on any reasonable basis, thus freeing Pakistan's great energy and influence for use elsewhere and giving Indian opponents of neutralism a chance to assert themselves.
3.	Bring Burma, Siam and free Viet-Nam into a southeast Asian alliance to include India and Pakistan as soon as either is ready to join.
4.	Extend the new Pacific pact between the United States, New Zealand and Australia to include the Philippines and a rearmed Japan. At the appropriate time, link it with the southeast Asian alliance.
5.	Instead of recognizing red China, create all possible difficulties for that regime. This means supporting Chiang Kai-shek on Formosa and encouraging any other anti-communist forces that emerge.
6.	Urge the Japanese, once they again become independent, to create a sizable military force as quickly as possible.
I believe that carrying out these six undertakings, or most of them, would save Asia-and that nothing less will.
Now, sir, for the remainder of my time I should like to devote some attention first of all to the amendment to the amendment introduced by the C.C.F., and lastly to the fisheries situation in Newfoundland. May I first of all deal with the amendment to the amendment which asks for the immediate introduction of national health insurance. It seems to me that the C.C.F. party is out to get this during this session for some reason or other. I notice from the reports that have been filed by the different provinces that Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan seem to favour the idea, but the other provinces do not. Newfoundland is the only province which has not reported up to the present time, but my understanding of the situation there is that it would be chaotic to introduce national health insurance at the present time.
Hon. members from Alberta and Saskatchewan, the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low), the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) all have spoken about the wonderful progress that has been made in their provinces. I think representatives from all provinces could give a similar story. I know that in Newfoundland, going back as far as 1934, we can tell a story of almost the elimination of tuberculosis as a major cause of death; the erection of 26 cottage hospitals, and the extension of hospital and medical facilities to at least 60 per cent of the people. But, although a great number of beds have


been provided in the past ten years, they are certainly not yet sufficient to justify an all-out health insurance plan.
I think the matter was considered by the people of Ontario in the election last year. The leader of the Liberal party went to the country at that time with a national health insurance plan as his chief policy. The premier of Ontario said it would be a fraud upon the people to allow them to think that such a program could be put into force at that time. Neither could it. Therefore it seems to me that the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is the wisest course for this country to pursue.
Members of the Liberal party have suggested that we should have a committee of the house. That would not go far enough; for it is necessary to have concurrence between the governments of the different provinces and the principal municipalities that operate hospitals and have to do with health matters. Therefore it seems to me that until the C.C.F. party can show how it can be done, the best way would be to hold a conference between representatives of the dominion government, the provinces, the municipalities and the medical profession, as outlined by the Leader of the Opposition in his speech the other day.
I should like to refer to the fisheries situation at this time. I am glad the minister is present while I am making these remarks. I know he is interested. I know that already he has sent the deputy minister down to Newfoundland to look over the situation, and I suppose he has brought back a report.
Perhaps what I have to say is an analysis of what has been happening during the last few years, but I think it is just as well that we should have it in summary form. There has been in Newfoundland in the last ten or twelve years a distinct trend toward the development of fresh fish markets, especially in the United States. During the war we had a big fresh fish market in Great Britain, but that is now completely lost, so that we are dependent now upon the fresh fish market in the United States. Emphasis has been directed toward this by the government of Newfoundland, with the result that everyone is fresh-fish minded.
It seems to me, however, that a word of caution is necessary, because what the United States gives now the United States can take away by the stroke of a pen, by the alteration of the tariff. In that way the fresh fish market could be lost. We should know that in Gloucester there are fish interests deeply concerned with the entry of Canadian fish on the United States market, and at any time they may ask the United States

government to make it more difficult for Canadian and other foreign fish to enter that market.
There can be no doubt that the United States market has been beneficial to the fisheries of Newfoundland, generally speaking. However it has helped to bring about a decline in the salt codfish industry. The salt cod fisheries constitute an industry which has existed since the days of discovery by Cabot. He brought back his report stating that the waters around the new land, around Newfoundland, were teeming with cod. People from England, from Spain and from Portugal, as well as from France, visited there every year. They have been coming out from Spain, Portugal and France almost every year since that time, with the exception of the war years. All those people have been interested in the salt cod fisheries.
As Newfoundland developed, the salt cod fisheries became the staple industry. It can no longer be regarded as the principal industry of Newfoundland, however, because one brings to mind the great volume of paper produced, and the increasing wealth due to the discovery and operation of mines producing mineral ores. Nevertheless the salt codfish industry is regarded very highly, because so many people take part in the salt cod fisheries. These people have their homes situated around the numerous bays and inlets and harbours along the six thousand miles of coast line. They have little gardens and farms which, with the fisheries, give them a very comfortable living in most cases.
The cod fisheries declined for the following reasons, it seems to me. First of all there were the effects of the war. Many enlisted, left their homes and did not return. Then there has been the construction by the United States government as well as by the Canadian government of defence bases in Newfoundland. Especially since the war there has been a great expansion of United States forces there. All this has drawn thousands of people away from the fisheries. I was surprised recently to be in several fishing villages and find them eating fish bought in St. John's. There was not a boat on the beach, not a fisherman in the place. Then hundreds more are going to Seven Islands to work on the railway, and to do such other work as is necessary for the development of the iron ore deposits found along the border between Quebec and Labrador.
In addition there has been a program of government industrial spending. In my opinion the government of Newfoundland has very unwisely gone into the experiment of starting business enterprises, establishing a
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne cement plant, gypsum plant, hardwood plant, machine plant and the like, the outcome of which to say the least is very problematical. Nevertheless it has drawn many people away from the fisheries. Indeed this was a deliberate policy intended to take people from the fisheries.
We remember, too, the low prices of 1950. In that year the prices of fish were the lowest they had been in ten years. Many were discouraged and did not return to the fisheries in 1951 or since. Then the government of Canada made the stipulation that it would not give any assistance, through the fisheries prices support board, to any fisherman who decided to go to Labrador and take part in the Labrador fisheries. If they did so it would be at their own risk.
Then there has been the loss of markets due to exchange. Brazil, a country in South America with a population of 53 million people, used to buy thousands of quintals of our fish, but has not been buying it recently. Spain has not been buying our fish, and this year we had to practically beg the Portuguese government to buy some of it. The situation is changed, and this has had a great effect upon our people. I think therefore the minister has a difficult task ahead of him. I have every sympathy for him, and I shall be glad to help in any way I can.
The government of Newfoundland, in conjunction with that of the dominion, has been making experiments in the manner of catching fish. I believe it was the provincial government that was responsible for the idea that people must get away from the slavery of producing salt codfish. "Slavery" was the word used by the premier of the province. I do not agree with him at all; I think it produces a most unwise psychological approach. However, four boats were brought from Iceland. The experiment cost $450,000. The Icelanders were going to show the Newfoundlanders how to catch fish. The boats are down at St. John's harbour now, and anyone who looks at them will say, "How did they happen to bring out these four tubs?"
That experiment failed. Then they introduced long liners. I believe the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) cherishes the idea that the long liners are going to be the solution of the difficulties of fishermen in Newfoundland. The federal and provincial governments have been experimenting with these long liners. I believe the provincial government has now abandoned the experiment and switched over to the Danish seine, so that the Danes can teach us how to fish. The federal government had the misfortune to have one of their long liner vessels blow up last year. There has not been sufficient data published to

The Address-Mr. IV. J. Browne enable us to judge the value of these experiments. I have no doubt that probably managed with a small crew, if the boat and the equipment do not cost too much, operations of that kind might prove profitable; but I cannot see how it could ever replace cod fishing operations with the use of traps, where in a month or two people can catch 800, 900 or 1,000 quintals of fish, a quintal being 112 pounds of dried fish.
In addition to this problem connected with experiments, within the next year or so the minister will have to face the problem of the marketing of codfish. The marketing of salt cod is always a difficult problem. In the old days, when we had free trade, it is notorious that merchants would undersell one another; and on one occasion at the close of the first world war there was chaos in the salt codfish industry because of this marketing difficulty.
In 1936, at the time of the commission of government, a fisheries board was set up. It was later on agreed that the merchants should have exclusive control of the marketing of salt codfish, and that this control would be under an organization known as the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited. That body still has the right to export fish. It is composed entirely of merchants, and hon. members will have some idea as to the organization itself when I state that it costs $10,000 to join it. Only a wealthy merchant can belong to the organization.
Therefore eventually all fish must come to the members who export it. A 3 per cent charge is made, and put in the coffers of NAFEL. Whether those concerned make the distribution or not, I cannot say. When the deputy minister of fisheries, Mr. Bates, was in St. John's recently, he threw out a suggestion that he would like to know what the fishermen wanted. Do they want to continue this method of exporting their fish, or what do they want?
His invitation was taken up by the Daily News, and in an article on November 8 it said that there seemed to be only two alternatives to the association which exists at present. There would have to be either a fishermen's marketing co-operative or a board. It seems to me that the board they had in mind was something along the lines of the wheat board in western Canada. Because I was interested in the matter I took time to look up the constitution of the board which was organized under the act passed in 1935 by the Bennett government. I read it through and it seemed to me that the idea was sound, that if a board could handle the export of millions of bushels of

wheat a similar board could handle the export of a million quintals of salt codfish from Newfoundland.
There is in Newfoundland at the present time another organization which has a great deal to say about fisheries matters, and I refer to the fishermen's federation. Some hon. members will remember that on February 6, 1951, I made a speech during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne during which I discussed the fisheries of Newfoundland and recommended that the government should follow the example that was set in 1929 when a commission recommended the teaching of co-operative methods to the fishermen. I suggested that Dr. Coady should be sent to Newfoundland to establish a school for the training of fishermen in cd-operative methods. The provincial government took up the idea, got Dr. Coady down there and subsidized the formation of the fishermen's federation which now has ten to fifteen thousand fishermen members all around Newfoundland. The majority of the .men interested in the catching of salt codfish, and fresh fish as well, are members of this federation. According to an article in the Daily News of August 8, 1951, Mr. Lane, the secretary of the federation, indicated that the federation was opposed to the continuation of the NAFEL organization.
I notice that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) was down there recently and said that this organization was there to stay. I did not read the full report of what he said, but I did read the comments made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) the other day in answer to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). I believe the situation is still fluid and I hope the minister is giving consideration to what will be best for the fishermen. That is the criterion that should always be used in connection with the fisheries of Newfoundland: what is going to be best for the fishermen.
There are three things that can be done. The present association can be continued or fishermen's marketing co-operatives can be set up. I am sure the minister will realize that that involves a lot of teaching, as it would be an educational process. It is not something that can be done in a day. It will take some time to train these men in the principles of co-operation, although during the past twelve or fifteen years many of them have become familiar with co-operative methods in buying and in the operation of credit societies. They have not had a great deal of experience with co-operative marketing. The third thing would be to set up a board similar to the wheat board. Eventually the minister will have to decide which is

best. I do not know which would be the best at the present time. Under the terms of union the present fisheries board continues for five years after April 1, 1949, so it will cease operations on April 1, 1954 unless legislation is brought in to continue it.
There was one other criticism in the Daily News article to which I referred. They said that the deputy minister seemed to be overlooking the premier of the province, that he did not consult with the government but asked only for suggestions from the public and the press as to what future methods of marketing should be adopted in Newfoundland. As the federal government has the responsibility in regard to fisheries it seems to me there was nothing that should arouse great objection by anybody in his simply asking for suggestions.
I am not prepared at the present time to say which is the best, but I do feel that the criterion I mentioned before, that is, what is going to be for the best interests of the fishermen, should be followed. No doubt the minister since taking over his office has realized something of the difficulties that exist down there.
Before I conclude I should like to draw his attention to certain other features of the situation facing the fisheries in Newfoundland.
He knows that trawlers and bankers come out from Portugal, Spain and France every year in hundreds. Most of these are sailing vessels with diesel power and they carry from 50 to 75 dories, which means that there are 50 to 75 fishermen because one fisherman goes out in a dory. The speech from the throne forecasts that legislation is to be introduced in connection with these Portuguese and Spanish fishermen coming into Newfoundland ports for bait and supplies.
This practice was stopped on July 1 as far as the other maritime provinces are concerned, but because Newfoundland at the time of union had an agreement with these countries permitting these fishermen to come into Newfoundland ports, the practice was continued there. I do not know if it is the intention of the government to forbid these vessels coming into Newfoundland ports, but I urge the minister to give earnest consideration to the matter before he refuses them entrance.
These are very industrious people. They undergo great hardship. They are brave men fishing the hard way, and they cause no trouble in St. John's. Many of them are married men with families and they live in countries where the standard of living is much lower than ours. Therefore I suggest that consideration be given to the problem before a hard and fast rule is laid down that
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne they be not allowed to come into Newfoundland ports to purchase bait and supplies as they have been doing for so many years.
The Portuguese government has taken a great interest in their fishermen to see that they have the latest boats and equipment. It looks after their welfare at home by providing houses, maternity benefits for wives and recreational benefits for the fishermen and their families. No one seems to be taking a similar interest in the fishermen of Newfoundland.
On previous occasions I have drawn attention to the benefits which are available to the farmers of western Canada, and other regions too, through farm improvement loans. The farmers of Newfoundland have received very little benefit from this legislation because for some reason or another they have not been able to get loans. The fishermen of Canada have no benefits under any comparable act. I believe the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) has a resolution on the order paper asking that the government give consideration to providing advantages for the fishermen similar to those being provided for our farmers.
Does it not seem strange that thousands of houses are going up in and around our cities at a cost of millions of dollars provided either by the government or government agencies, when nothing is being provided for the thousands and thousands of fishermen who live in small places, merely because they are not located on serviced land. It will be a thousand years before they will have serviced land in some of these small settlements. It is impossible. Yet does it not seem unfair that the privilege of being able to borrow a sum of money to improve their means of earning a livelihood or to improve their homes is denied them? It seems to me a sound proposition that a fisherman should be treated in such a manner as to enable him to obtain a loan of that kind. I know plenty of fishermen who, if they were given seven years to repay, would be very glad to get loans and improve their homes and their means of earning a livelihood.
Then there is the question of storm damage which was brought up in the house the other day, on which occasion the minister replied to a question by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter). This fall I was a witness of the after-effects of a storm. I stood on the cliff at the little village of St. Michaels, Ferryland. I looked out at the rough seas and saw pieces of boats, pieces of stages and wharves floating around and the fishermen on the beach trying to salvage what

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne they could. Only a village or two were affected at that time. The other day there was another storm of greater proportions which caused greater damage. As the result the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, whose district was more affected than that of anybody else, asked his question.
I understand the matter is under consideration by the government. The previous minister told us that he was considering a method of two-way insurance involving the federal and provincial governments, and perhaps the fishermen concerned as well, so that when damage of that kind was suffered the fishermen would be insured and would be able to rehabilitate themselves without delay. I do not know what is going to happen now, but I do know that whether a storm is nationwide or only affects one or two villages it is most disastrous for the fishermen concerned.

Mr. Speaker, coming from British Columbia, as I do, I think I may say that all agree that two better appointments could not have been made than the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and the present Solicitor General (Mr. Campney). British Columbia is a young province and deserves the type of representation these two young men will give it. I wish to discuss first the amendment to the amendment in the name of the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell) which reads in part as follows:
We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed: (a) to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program.
It seems to me that no one is more qualified to speak about health and hospitalization than a member from British Columbia. We have seen confusion over the years not only under the present government but under the former government which was made up in part of representatives of the Liberal party. I do not think anything was the matter with hospitalization in British Columbia in the first place. The idea was good. The trouble with the administration was that the plan was introduced a year or two too soon. Because of the insistence of certain gentlemen in authority, the law was introduced and the hospitalization plan came into being in British Columbia before we were ready for it.

In the first instance the premiums were set at a rather low level, and my recollection is that they were increased two or three times. We found that the hospitals of British Columbia were not built to take care of the influx arising from the increased number of patients. We found that our nursing schools could not take care of the necessary nursing staffs required for a hospitalization scheme of the type instituted in British Columbia. We found that the cost of construction of new hospitals was, as the Social Credit minister of health and welfare said the other day in the provincial capital, "beyond the power of the people of British Columbia to support." Nowhere at any time will there be as good an example as the hospitalization scheme in British Columbia of something being done long before the proper time and without proper investigation.
As I say, the idea was good. I do not think anyone in British Columbia would argue that the hospitalization plan as we now know it in that province does not benefit the type of people who should receive benefit, people who cannot afford to pay their hospital bills in the first place. However, it is an outstanding example of a government doing something before the people first of all were prepared to accept the extra load on their tax bills and second, before the government knew how to give proper administration covering a matter of that kind. We have confusion in British Columbia so far as hospitalization is concerned. The present government went into office not only because of the things the coalition did not do but because they said that immediately upon taking office the hospitalization plan would become a voluntary scheme. Gone would be the premiums, gone would be the extra taxes, but anyone who wanted to belong to the hospitalization scheme could do so on a contributory basis. If you didn't want to belong to it and wanted to pay your hospital bills in the regular way, why then they would be in agreement with that idea. I do not say this because my hon. friends of the Social Credit party are sitting across the house from me now. Except for one man, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), they did not have anything to do with the provincial set-up. I made it because I had an idea that this subamendment would be proposed by the C.C.F. party. I believe the idea is good, but I think they are a little before their time. Anyone coming from British Columbia can prove that a national health scheme now is years before its time. The people are not ready for it. If you took a vote on it throughout the country, beyond some misguided people who vote for the C.C.F., I do not think that too many would support it at this time.
I have much respect for the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He did say in his speech that he brought it to the attention of the house for their consideration. I think that was a fair statement and I do not think he took the subamendment too seriously himself. It will be a move toward the idea presented by my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) when he said the other day that he thought the best way to approach this was through a committee. I think he said a joint committee of the House and Senate, but at least he said a committee. That committee would fully investigate the matter and avoid the serious problem which we in British Columbia now face.
If the federal government takes on this national health program we will have not only the difficulties which exist in British Columbia, small as they may be nationally, but we will have to multiply those difficulties a hundredfold. I think nothing would be as tragic as for the government to embark on a national health program at this time, ill prepared as it is in regard to facilities, and with the people ill prepared to accept the cost that must result from the subamendment. I am going to vote against the subamendment not merely because it is a matter of nonconfidence in the government, which to my

mind is not too important, though I will say that if the subamendment had been worded a little differently I might have risen in my place and voted for it.

If the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) is quoted correctly in the Ottawa Citizen of December 6, he proposes to bring to the attention of the house this week a certain matter that happened in Korea during the visit of the next president of the United States. I was very surprised that the hon. member did not bring the matter to the attention of the government today, and if he had I would most likely not be making the remarks I am going to make.
In the Citizen of December 6 there is an article written by Bill Boss, Canadian Press staff reporter in Korea. I think I can say that he is a man with whom I have not always agreed when he reports on Korean incidents. Nevertheless he brought to the attention of the Canadian public, I think, the fact that a guard of honour in Korea, in which was included a number of Canadian troops, was held on a parade ground for seven hours. Perhaps this question and the discussion of it would have come better from

the opposition, but some of us in this house know exactly what this means. The article says this:
For Elsenhower's parade, scheduled at 3 p.m. the troops marched on to the airstrip at 1.15 p.m. They kept warm by beating their hands together, kicking their feet and pounding one another's backs.
The Canadians didn't complain, considering it an honour to be able to pay their respects to General Eisenhower. But there was much criticism by newspapermen over the lack of consideration shown the troops . . .
The Canadians evoked all-round admiration the hard way Wednesday. On the wind-swept airstrip in five above zero weather they discarded comfortable parkas to parade more efficiently in their beautifully pressed battledress.
The men decided on it themselves, suggesting to Hanson before the morning rehearsals: "You can't do arms drill properly wearing a parka!"
In consequence of that story, if the newspapers are correct, the next president of the United States has had to apologize to certain people in Korea for keeping our troops and other troops on a parade ground for seven hours. The hon. member for Nanaimo said that he was going to bring this matter before the House of Commons, and I quite agree that he should do so. But before he does it, may 1 say that I remember standing on a parade ground, with some hundreds of men, for five and a half hours one day waiting for the hon. member for Nanaimo; and I must say that when he arrived on that parade ground he was on time. I happened to be the sergeant major on the parade at that time. I checked the parade and found that he was a minute and a half late. I took issue with certain senior officers at that time, just as I take issue now. I do not expect for a moment that a Canadian officer was in charge of that Korean guard of honour, but I suggest that there was a Canadian officer in charge of the Canadian men in that composite guard.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, officers are funny people. You may have a man who works at a desk and who, when he gets home at night, walks the dog around the block, is run by his wife and children, and has Milquetoast tastes in his daily habits; but when, all of a sudden, you put a pip on his shoulder he becomes a roaring lion. I have known officers of this type. Thank goodness they are few in number. I am quite sure that they do not include any former army officer in this House of Commons, but there are some of this type in the Canadian army. I do not say that this man Hanson, who cannot defend himself-and I am certainly not going to attack him here-is that type or is responsible, but somebody is responsible for keeping those Canadian troops on the parade ground for seven hours; and then to have the audacity to tell me, one who has had a little bit to do with troops, that Canadian troops said: "We want to do small arms drill
The Address-Mr. Goode without parkas at five below zero" is something I cannot understand, having regard to the stupidity of it. I think this is the worst type of reporting possible.
I have complained about this gentleman before. You will remember that I said something about casualties being mentioned in the paper, or units being mentioned in the paper, before the people at home knew about it, so that we could save some of our mothers and our wives in Canada unnecessary trouble and worry. This is the same gentleman. He tells us now that Canadians, in newly pressed serge, wanted to do parade ground drill in battledress rather than use parkas. Most of us know that is not true. Nevertheless, this is true: Canadian troops along with others were held on the parade ground for several hours at practically zero temperatures.
I do not say this is a responsibility of government. Goodness knows the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) does not know everything that goes on with regard to these minor matters, although he does in most major matters; but I think an investigation should be started immediately, when the next president of the United States is practically forced to make an apology; when he himself arrives at the parade ground immediately upon the proper time that is appointed; and we have taken seven hours to put a few men on a guard of honour.
I was a member of the Canadian forces and did not do nearly as much as did most of the veterans in this House of Commons. But I will guarantee now that I can take a thousand men on a guard of honour and put them in their proper positions in half an hour; and I know of no sergeant major in the Canadian army-especially in the regular Canadian army-who could not do it in 15 minutes. I think there were perhaps some thirty or forty men on this guard of honour, although I do not know; but there is not a sergeant major in the Canadian army who could not have done it in a quarter of an hour. Yet this article says we kept our troops rehearsing for seven hours. A Canadian infantryman, after he has been in the army for six months, knows more about small arms drill than do most soldiers in other armies. I think it has been recognized that the Canadian soldier is a specialist in small arms. Yet we have to take seven hours before a guard of honour is held, so these boys can learn basic training that they most likely knew two years previously.
I would suggest to the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) that this occurrence be fully investigated. I am going to ask more questions about it in the house. I want to know why Canadian troops were

The Address-Mr. Goode held there for seven hours, on whose orders they were held there, and who was the senior Canadian officer on that parade.
Having said something that perhaps might be construed as against the Department of National Defence-although it is not so intended-I think this also should be said, because in regard to the same department we have heard many things this session as to the shortcomings of certain officials. I have here quite a long article which was printed in the New York Times of Monday, November 10, 1952, and I propose to put it on the record. It will take about ten minutes, but I think it should be put on the record now. This is an article written in France by a staff reporter of the New York Times. It reads as follows:
Quietly and efficiently the Canadians have developed a jet fighter base here in the last four months that will compare-in speed of construction, operational efficiency and living conditions for officers and men-with any of the twenty-one other North Atlantic Treaty Organization air bases already built in France.
This is the home of the alliance's first F-86E Sabre jet fighter wing on the European continent, and all sixty of the Sabres here are Canadian-built. Manned entirely by regulars of the second Canadian Air Force fighter wing, the Canadian group is the first of four such wings scheduled to be flown to the continent during the next eighteen months to join the allied air forces, central Europe, under Lieut.-General Lauris Norstad of the United States air forces.
This 1,000-acre Canadian base is more than just a technical installation; it is an example in co-operation between Canada and France that can be held up to the United States in its heavy task of building a chain of air bases in foreign lands for the defence of the free world.
The progress being made here would be outstanding by any test. On July 3, for instance, there was nothing to see here but a French-built 8,000-foot concrete fighter runway, a parallel taxiway, other hard-surface areas and a few hangars.
Now, four months later, French civil engineers, working with Canadian plans, have built sixty new aluminum-sheathed prefabricated buildings that already house nearly 1,000 Canadian officers and men plus operational equipment and supplies. Another 1,000 Canadians are due to arrive in the coming year.
As autumn rains and cold sweep over this bare tableland in the Moselle valley the Canadian personnel are comfortably installed in steam heated, insulated French-built prefabs, each of which can house 104 officers or men or can be used as recreational halls, administration buildings, chapels, mess halls or supply quarters. Each building, shaped like a giant H, costs approximately $88,000.
"We are very pleased with French materials and construction work," Group Capt. C. F. Johns, Canadian construction supervisor, said yesterday, "These buildings compare well with our own air stations in Canada."
Under the Atlantic pact organization's rules, France selects the sites and builds the runways and some hangars for the organization's air bases in France, but then the country whose air unit uses the fields must build its own barracks, warehouses, recreation halls, etc. It now appears that the Canadians have avoided some of the pitfalls that have delayed the United States' base building here.

The Canadians' progress seems to be due to three factors: Close preparation and co-operation with the French before the earth was turned; a delegation of real authority from Ottawa to Canadian officials sent to France to supervise the work; and diplomacy in dealing with the French from the government down to the local contractor. The combination of the three has paid dividends.
The Canadian air force made a close study of French building techniques long before it sent its first Sabre wing to Grostenquin on Oct. 11. It knew back in Ottawa a year ago what the French could build well and what they should not be expected to build.
When the Canadian air force started drawing up detailed plans and specifications for barracks and other semi-permanent buildings last winter it checked these with engineers in the French embassy in Ottawa. It then completed plans in both English and French and in both the inch-scale and the metric scale used on the continent. When the plans were finally laid before the French government and its engineers and civil contractors in the spring, all knew just what the Canadians wanted. The French reacted sympathetically from the start.
Some of the most experienced construction engineers in the United States have been hired by the United States air force to come to Europe and spend at least one year until October, 1953, supervising building work on three American Atlantic pact bases in France.
Some of this group of technicians have flown up to the Canadian base to look for new ideas. It is too early for their full recommendations, but they have already noted by comparison two major weaknesses in the present American way of base building in France.
That is an example to the rest of the world. Therefore in saying something about some Canadian officers who are in a very small minority, I also wish to congratulate those permanent force officers who are doing such a wonderful job, and who are in a large majority in our forces in Canada.
I have two matters concerning my own riding that I wish to speak on for a moment. One has to do with the fishing industry on the Fraser river. This also concerns the hon. members for New Westminster (Mr. Mott) and Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). Most likely in their turn they will speak on the same matter, and perhaps do a much better job than I. I wish to take a few minutes to bring to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) the marketing conditions in Canada as far as canned salmon is concerned. The hon. member who spoke before me referred to the condition of fisheries on the east coast. A like condition prevails now in British Columbia. We are starting an overlay of warehouse stocks of canned salmon of high grade, and before the next fishing season something must be done for the Canadian salmon industry, at least in some way to help them to finance through the next year.	[DOT]
I am not going to suggest to the Minister of Fisheries what should be done, but I do say to him that conditions, especially among

some of the packers in regard to their debts to the bank, are getting to the point where I am sure the federal government will have to step in. I have said during my time at home between sessions that perhaps a subsidy to the fishing industry might be the final solution. I am not too sure of that now. It could be, but a man in this position, representing 6,000 or 7,000 fishermen, as the members from British Columbia do, must go very carefully in making statements that could be wrong. I do not say that my subsidy idea is wrong, but I want to leave it open to the Minister of Fisheries to make up his own mind, perhaps after conversations with the rest of us, as to what should be done for the canned salmon industry in British Columbia. I am sure some veterans with fishing boats are going to be in dire circumstances by the end of next year unless in some way we step in to finance the surplus warehouse stocks of canned salmon we now have throughout Canada.
I do not think the government should step in at this moment to make a large loan, or anything of that kind. Perhaps they could purchase some stocks on condition that the fishing industry find extra markets. But, as I say, these small suggestions from me are not in any way meant to influence, and certainly will not in any way influence the Minister of Fisheries in his final analysis of the situation. I do hope, however, that our fishermen in British Columbia will be assured of at least a reasonable resale market for their fish in 1953.
In conclusion I should like to touch on one other matter. As we all know the Canadian Legion has asked each of us, both at home and here, either to support or go against their brief. We all know what that brief is. Some of us are prepared to support it; some of us are not. I have always found the Legion, especially in my own riding, to be pretty reasonable men. There is no doubt in my mind that the recipients of war veterans' allowance, in some instances, are having a pretty tough time. I would suggest to the minister that until another session comes on and another veterans affairs committee is set up, this $10 from the assistance fund that we give to some under a means test-and some we do not give it to at all- should be added to the war veterans' allowance without the means test; that is, without that second means test. Let us add that $10 to the basic rate. It may not be very much, but I know of cases where that $10 would just mean the difference this year between a decent Christmas for some of our older veterans and a Christmas that might mean going somewhere other than their own home for a meal.
The Address-Mr. Quelch
I want to say this to the Minister of Public Works. The Fraser river concerns British Columbia members. I wish only to speak about my own part that borders the municipality of Richmond. Rightly or wrongly the engineers of the department at New Westminster decided on a scheme which will narrow the Fraser river so as to allow the current to carry the silt out into the Pacific and, so far as I can see, their plan is a good one. Across from Richmond at the moment, on the south side of the river, they have put in many hundreds of thousands of tons of rock, and have fortified that southern bank. In doing this they have pushed the strong part of the current over to the north side of the river, bordering on the municipality of Richmond.
All there is at that point at the moment to hold the water is an old dike built many years before my time. I suggest to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) that that dike will not hold at the time of the next Fraser river freshet, should we have normal snow at the headwaters of the Fraser. I would ask him to co-operate with the reeve and council of the municipality of Richmond to do something to strengthen the north side of the river; because if the freshet ever breaks through that dike we are going to have a crisis on our hands that will cost many millions of dollars. If the Fraser river breaks through the dike, and if the water is sufficiently high, as it usually is at the time of a freshet, the water could proceed almost to the locality of Brighouse, and many thousands of people would be affected. I suggest investigation of the matter should be made now because, as most of us from British Columbia know, it will not be too long before the Fraser river will go on its yearly rampage.

The minister was also critical of the fact that municipal debt in Alberta has been increasing. The same would be true of the municipalities in any other province. There is a definite reason why the debts of the municipalities in Alberta have been increasing. It is largely due to the fact that municipalities throughout the province are taking advantage of the credit that is made available by the Alberta government at the rate of only 2 per cent under the self-liquidating projects legislation. These loans are granted at 2 per cent with repayment spread over a period of 20 years.
Many municipalities throughout Alberta, and I am glad it is so, are taking advantage of this legislation in order to put in water systems, sewage disposal plants and other services. I think we will all agree that this is definitely to the advantage of the people because it makes it easier for them to carry on in their homes, and makes conditions far more healthy than is the case in small towns where there is no water available in the homes. I was interested in an article which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of November 1, 1951 dealing with this matter, which reads:
Twenty-seven Alberta municipal governments have been granted 2 per cent loans totalling $4,770,950 from the Alberta self-liquidating projects fund since March 31, it was stated by Kenneth Hawkins, deputy provincial treasurer.
A total of $7,000,000 was voted for the fund by the legislature this year, and more than $2,500,000

remains to be lent to local governments to finance self-liquida ting projects such as installation of water and sewer systems.
The Alberta self-liquidating projects act was passed two years ago, and during the first year almost $5,000,000 was lent to the local governments, so the total amount lent by the fund is approaching $10,000,000. In the initial year, loans numbered 34 and totalled $4,978,353.
That was as at November 1, 1951, and I understand that since that time additional loans amounting to $6 million have been granted, making a total of $16 million at 2 per cent. I am quite sure that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will not criticize such a policy because it is to the advantage of Alberta. Mind you, this is not something imposed upon the people; it is done at their own request. A plebiscite is held to determine whether or not the debt will be incurred in order to instal water systems or other services. It is only after it has been voted upon that a loan can be made.
I suggest that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys would be doing a service to his province and to the people of Canada if he would put pressure upon the federal government to adopt a similar policy in regard to loans in connection with federal projects.
1	believe there is still legislation on the statute books to provide for the granting of municipal improvement assistance with loans at the rate of 2 per cent. That legislation was suspended during the war and no loans have been made under it since that time. I think the minister should put pressure upon the federal government to once more make these loans available.
It is true that municipalities in Alberta can get money from the provincial government at
2	per cent, but that is not the case in the majority of the other provinces. If a municipality wants to finance a project of this kind it has to pay 4J or 5 per cent or even a higher interest rate. Let me go a step further.
