I think most hon. members will agree that the present situation in agriculture is a matter for grave concern. Certainly the farmers themselves are concerned about the situation. I say that because in spite of the fact that there have been two record crops in the west, farm income is down 5 per cent this year. That is largely due to the fact that the price received for farm products has dropped by 10 per cent while at the same time the cost of those things the farmer has to buy has gone up by approximately 5 per cent. My authority for that statement is to be found in the "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada, November, 1952", where on page 9 there is the following:
Farm income.-Although farm cash income from the sale of farm products and from participation payments, including those on previous years' crops, may reach a new all-time high, it is estimated that a lower income in kind, reduced values of year-end inventory changes and higher operating costs will serve to provide a net farm income about 5 per cent below that of a year ago.
On the next page under the heading "Farm Prices of Agricultural Products" I read the following:
With the exception of the month of January, the index of farm prices of agricultural products was substantially lower during the first eight months of 1952 than for the corresponding period of 1951 . . . Even if the present level of the index can be maintained until the end of the year, it is estimated that the annual average for 1952 will be at least 10 per cent below that of a year ago.
Under the heading "Prices of Commodities and Services Used by Farmers" I read the following:
Prices paid by farmers for commodities and services used for production and for living continued to rise during 1952. The composite price index number of goods, service and cost of living in 1952 is nearly 5 per cent above that for 1951 with the greatest increase occurring in farm wages followed closely by family living costs, equipment and materials.
I should like to point out that if it had not been for the large crops that were harvested in the west the drop in income would have been considerably greater than 5 per cent. But we cannot always expect the kind of crops we have had out there for the

The Address-Mr. Quelch past two years. The present situation is causing a good deal of concern already. The moisture content in the soil today is about 70 per cent of normal and unless there is very heavy rainfall between now and next June we cannot hope for a crop next year anything like those we have had during the past two years.
I will admit frankly that the condition of the grain grower is far better than that of the livestock man. It is the livestock man who is really taking the beating in Canada today. I have in mind the hog producer, the poultry producer and the dairy producer. These men are really hard hit. The cost of their feed is high and the price of the things they have to sell is falling fast. The result is that today there is a good deal of talk among farm organizations about the need, and even the desirability, of reducing production of their commodities. In that connection I should like to refer to the issue of the Rural Co-operator under date of November 25, 1952. On the front page under the heading "Time to cut production?" there is the following:
Regulated production or government assistance are the two courses open to farmers, C. A. Milligan, Napanee, president of the Ontario federation of agriculture, said in an address at the recent annual meeting of the Ontario cream producers association in Toronto. The farmer cannot continue to produce on today's prices, Mr. Milligan said. He posed the question of whether it might not be the time to cut production to domestic requirements to insure a fair price.
If the government is not prepared to maintain agricultural prices at a level that will bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities, then it would seem that the only solution for farmers is to reduce their production. If farmers are going to be forced to operate under the so-called law of supply and demand, then of course the logical thing for them is to play the game according to the law of supply and demand and cut down their production, thus reducing supply so that demand will catch up with supply and prices will rise. That is what the manufacturers do. That is what they did during the depression years. They did not reduce their prices in order to try to increase sales. They reduced their production, and while the prices of agricultural products fell in those years by 65 per cent the prices of manufactured goods only fell by 25 per cent during the same period as a result of the manufacturers operating under the so-called law of supply and demand.
Let me make this point. If the farmers adopt a policy of that kind, if they do reduce their production, then the federal government will have to take the full responsibility for that action. If farmers today, in the face


of the world situation, reduce their production then that will be an extremely vicious policy and, as I say, the federal government will have to take the responsibility for it. I would say that if such action is taken it will be the result of a breach of faith on the part of the federal government.
In the first place I would point out that a reduction in production cannot possibly be justified in the face of the present world situation. We heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) speak this afternoon and the picture he painted was somewhat gloomy. He told us about the difficulties of the have-not nations and the difficulty of making supplies available to them. I was very much struck by an article written recently by Dr. Hugh Keenleyside, former deputy minister of mines and resources. I understand he is head of the United Nations technical assistance program. The article is published in the December 6 issue of Saturday Night. I am going to quote from it because, while I realize that some members will have read it, there are many others, no doubt, who have not read it. I think the article brings out some very important points which should be given careful consideration by hon. members and by the government. The heading of the article is, "Is Military Defence Enough?" I read from page 23 as follows:
There can be valid arguments as to the amount of effort and the precise allocation of our resources that should be devoted to each aspect of this basic problem. It is argued by some of our political leaders that, as far as Canada is concerned, the present division of approximately $100 for direct defence to $1 for technical and economic aid to the fermenting and revolutionary areas of the world is about right.
To many others such a distribution of our democratic resources seems dangerously unrealistic. This view is shared by the commission on foreign economic policy appointed under the chairmanship of Mr. Nelson Rockefeller by the president of the United States, and by a whole galaxy of equally distinguished and equally conservative statesmen and economists.
It can be and is argued that in the case of Canada our people are not prepared to make the additional financial sacrifices that would be necessary to provide both kinds of protection. At the moment that may be true. But that is not necessarily the final word of the Canadian people on this subject.
Our government has worked with great courage, skill and persistence to convince the Canadian people that guns are necessary. I am satisfied that a similar persistence, skill and courage would produce a similar response on our other defensive front. This is a time for leadership, not for simple compliance with existing opinion. If the public knew the facts, opinion might change. Popularity is not the final test of governmental greatness. What are some of these facts that the public should know? Well, let's look at the world around us.

I am going to cite two examples that he gives. He says:
Half the people in the world are ill, and expect to die before reaching the age of 35. But they know that they could and should be cured, and that if they were Canadians or New Zealanders or Swedes they would probably live to the age of 70.
Half the people in the world have an income of less than $100 a year; or, in other words, most of the people in the world are hungry most of the time. But they know that there could be enough food, and enough clothing and shelter, for all.
This article states that perhaps public opinion is not ready for this, but it points out that if people were educated with respect to what the situation is in the world they would no doubt support greater economic aid. Well, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) told the people in Edmonton that down in Ottawa they had a bunch of statesmen, not politicians. Surely if the cabinet is composed of a bunch of statesmen they would be prepared to risk their reputation on a policy of economic aid instead of just going along as far as they thought the people might support them. The people at this time need leaders and not merely men who will follow general public opinion.
Now the question is, in the light of that situation can reduced production of food be possibly justified? I am satisfied that the vast majority of people in Canada knowing of the situation would say that the answer is no. No doubt increased production of food and its distribution to hungry people would be one of the greatest weapons we could use to keep peace. Government policy should be to encourage an increase in the production of food, not a decrease. Unfortunately there might very well be a decrease unless the government gives some kind of a guarantee to agriculture that in the event of their increasing production they will not have to take a reduced price, which may mean they will have to take a lesser price for their increased production than they would receive for the decreased production.
The article by Dr. Keenleyside suggests that it might mean some sacrifices. I would suggest that by maintaining a high level of production, and furthermore by expanding production, in this country we would actually have an increase in prosperity. Certainly you would have greater prosperity than you would by allowing decreased production. No country can become prosperous by decreasing its' production.
Some people will say: Well, if we are going to give some of that production to other nations, does that not necessarily mean increased taxation? I would say, in the light of the situation in Canada today, that the
The Address-Mr. Quelcb total cost of aid given to foreign nations would not have to be met by taxation. I would say that for this reason. We have a situation today where inventories in the country are building up. There are surpluses in many industries; there are surpluses in agriculture; the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) referred to a surplus of fish. You can go right down the line and find many surpluses. Unfortunately in many parts of Canada today we also find people with reduced purchasing power to buy the goods they require and hence we find buying on the instalment plan and credit buying has expanded very rapidly, for the simple reason that people have not the money and therefore they buy on time. That situation indicates a lack of effective demand.
We have a certain amount of unemployment and undeveloped resources. In order to bring about the distribution of surplus goods the government would be justified in going to the Bank of Canada for funds, and not depending upon the borrowing of the savings of the people or increased taxation. That would mean a saving in interest charges and would not increase our debt burden.
I would say that the government has forced the farmers into a position where, in order to secure a good price, they have to reduce their production; and if that is so they will be guilty of a breach of faith with the farmers. I say so for this reason. It will be recalled by members who were in the house during the latter years of the war that price ceilings were placed on agricultural production. It was announced that that was part of a stabilizing program. The government asked the farm organizations to support that program, giving them the definite assurance that it would be part and parcel of a stabilization program under which prices of agricultural production would be stabilized after the war. The government also established the agricultural prices support board which was to prevent prices falling below a certain level.
As years went by the farm organizations were not satisfied that prices were being maintained at a fair level, and asked the government to establish a formula. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), when speaking to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in annual convention two years ago at Niagara, announced what the formula would be. At the last session he also announced the formula in the house. He said then that the support prices would be maintained so that the price of agricultural products today would bear the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as they existed in the base years, 1943, 1944, and 1945.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
Would anybody say that today prices are being maintained in line with that formula?
I was satisfied that such was not the case, and I wrote to the dominion bureau of statistics and asked what the price of agricultural products would be on the basis of that formula. I put this information on the record at the last session, but just to remind members I want to place a few figures on the record now.
On the basis of that formula the price of hogs would be $29.72 per hundred pounds. The support price is only $26, and I understand that in January the price is to be reduced to $23. What possible justification can there be for reducing that price from $26 to $23 when it is already 3 cents per pound below the formula, and when the price of everything else is going up?
Then we can take the price of eggs. Under the formula they should be 73 cents a dozen, but the floor price is 38 cents. The price of butter should be 64 cents per pound, but the floor price as of January of this year was 58 cents; it may have changed since then. On the basis of the formula farmers are perfectly justified in asking that the government maintain support prices at a higher level in order to assure them that the prices of farm produce today will bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities on the basis of the base years, 1943-45. I say that no stone should be left unturned by the government in order to expand production of food in order to help meet the tremendous need that exists in the world today and to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) referred this afternoon.
Now for a few minutes I wish to turn to the international wheat agreement, because the Agricultural Prices Support Act does not deal with wheat. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) said when he spoke in the house, we in this group would like to see a new international wheat agreement signed, but we insist on certain changes being made before it is signed. Certain weaknesses that exist in the agreement should be taken care of; and we were very glad to hear the minister state that he is going to strive for higher prices under the new agreement.
The main weaknesses I refer to under the international wheat agreement are these. It will be recalled that when the British wheat agreement was signed in 1945 most people were of the opinion that price levels were bound to go down. Everybody seemed to think that, and certainly the government thought it. So the British wheat agreement was signed; but instead of the price of everything going down the price of everything else went up and, as a result, the farmers took a
TMr. Quelch.j

beating. When the 1948 agreement came up, everybody again seemed to take it for granted that the price of everything was bound to go down and when the international wheat agreement was signed there was the provision in it that the floor price would drop 10 cents every year without regard to what happened to the price level.
At that time, speaking for this group, I warned of the danger of that provision. I pointed out that there was no assurance that price levels would go down, that it was quite possible prices would go up, and that if the price levels went up there was no reason why the floor price should go down. At that time I wanted the price of wheat under the international wheat agreement to be tied to the price levels of importing nations so that if the price of everything else went down the price of wheat would go down, but if the price of everything else went up then the price of wheat would go up too. The result of that would be that our exports of wheat to a particular country would bring back the same amount of imports to this country.
At that time there was no support from farm organizations for the suggestion we made in the house. I am glad to say, however, that today farm organizations are asking for that very thing, an escalator clause. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) must agree with that proposition, because I remember a speech by him some years ago in which he said he did not like to have to sell wheat in advance, without knowing what the price should be. He did not like to set the price ahead four years. When you set the price, as it is set under the international wheat agreement, you are merely guessing what the price should be. But if you set a price in the first year on a basis that seems fair in relation to the prices of other commodities, and then tie that price to the price level of other commodities, you are not guessing. You know that in the next few years the price of that wheat will still continue to bear a fair relation to the price of other commodities. Therefore in any wheat agreement that is signed I think there should be some provision-and I am not trying to be dogmatic about it-that would take care of that situation so that if in future instead of going down the price level went up, the farmer would not suffer as a consequence, as he has suffered under the international wheat agreement and under the British wheat agreement. I am hoping that some action will be taken along that line.
The price of wheat today is, of course, low as compared with the actual price of wheat

in 1948. In addition to that, the prices of the things the farmer has to buy have gone up considerably, putting the wheat grower in an unfavourable position. Although wheat does not come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, it is nevertheless interesting to note that if the formula announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), using the basis of 1943-44-45 were used in connection with wheat, the price today would be $2.53 a bushel, according to the bureau of statistics. I am not suggesting that we should try to get $2.53 a bushel. I merely mention that fact in order to show that the price of wheat today is low in comparison with the prices of other commodities. I am suggesting that, first of all, we should try to get a higher price-and the minister has assured us that he is going to try to get that-and have a higher floor. Then there should be a clause in the agreement which would make it possible to adjust those prices in relation to changing conditions. In other words, there should be some form of escalator clause.
I should also like to join with the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) in what he said about the wheat board. I think the wheat board have done a magnificent job under extremely difficult conditions. I know I speak for the people back in my constituency when I say that they have no desire to see the wheat board done away with. They want the wheat board to continue as a 100 per cent marketing agency. They do not want to be thrown back to the mercy of the vagaries of the grain exchange under which every time they try to expand production, they are penalized by reduced prices. The world today needs expansion of production and we must have a policy that will make it possible to have that expansion without penalizing the producers by reducing their prices.
I believe my time is rapidly being exhausted, but before concluding I should like to say a few words with regard to income tax. I see that the minister is in his seat. I am not going to say a great deal at this time because I know that the proper time to discuss this matter is in the budget debate, but I want to make a protest on behalf of the people I represent about a policy that was instituted this fall, and that caused a great deal of hard feeling.
About October a number of the farmers of my district received letters telling them to appear before a federal investigator at either Drumheller or Stettler, and to bring with them a full statement showing all expenditures and receipts, as well as their bank
The Address-Mr. Quelch books, the titles to any property they possessed, their bonds and everything else, dating back to the year 1946. You can understand just what the reaction of these farmers was. This is 1952. The department were going back to 1946. The situation caused a great deal of hard feeling, and they ran into all kinds of trouble. The first thing they ran into was this. When they went to the bank and wanted to get documents of title, the banks in many instances said no, we are not going to give you the titles; we are holding them as security; and you could not expect them to do so. The farmers arrived with only about half what the investigators wanted. In some cases I have heard from farmers that they were treated decently by the investigators. On the other hand some farmers have told me the opposite. I guess it depended on the position the farmer was in.
I suggest to the minister that, whether it was good policy or not, it was poor politics, just before an election, to pull off a stunt like that. Of course I am not a Liberal, so I am not worrying any; but I do not think it is good politics. If the letter written had just contained a line or two saying: "We want to help you with your income tax return; we do not think your statements are quite correct and if you will come down to the office, we will help you formulate it" there would not have been anything like the amount of hard feeling. But the content of the letter was to the effect: You have been doing something that is wrong, and we are going to find out what it is. There was a kind of dictatorial attitude that people do not like. As I say, it is poor politics.
There is one other case that I have had brought to my attention; it is the case of the housekeeper on the farm. The farmers feel that they should be allowed a deduction for the wages of a housekeeper. I know that matter was discussed in this house two or three years ago and it was not allowed; but this is one thing I wish the minister would take into consideration. A farmer is allowed a deduction for farm help; yet in many cases the person employed as a housekeeper is actually doing quite a large percentage of farm work, such as milking the cows, maybe, or looking after the poultry, feeding the pigs and so on. I suggested to one or two of the people who wrote to me that it had not been allowed in the past, but I would bring it to the attention of the minister again. I suggested in the meantime that if there was anybody employed on the farm in that way, instead of saying that the wages were $50, if she was working partly as housekeeper and partly as hired help, to put it in as $25 for
448	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith hired help and $25 for housekeeper. I do not know whether or not I was giving them advice that might get them into trouble. I told them that I did not have anything official to go on, but it looked to me like common sense. I hope the minister will give the matter consideration.
I believe that my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker, but before I sit down I should like to say this. I have made a plea asking that greater economic aid be given to certain foreign countries, to what are considered the "have-not" nations. That can be done without any sacrifice on the part of the people because it can be done out of an increase in production. But before we start to give greater aid to people in foreign countries we should first of all make sure that we are doing everything we can to look after our own people.
There is one class of people that I believe should have attention, and I think that attention is long overdue; I refer to that class of people who are physically incapacitated. Many resolutions have been introduced by private members, and I think by some on the other side of the house, with regard to this matter; and every hon. member of this house who has spoken on it has spoken sympathetically. If a free vote were taken tomorrow as to whether or not pensions should be granted to people who are physically incapacitated, I am satisfied that it would pass unanimously in this house. I hope the government will give consideration to the matter, because I am satisfied that a country such as Canada should be in a position to guarantee a fairly decent standard of living to all people provided they are willing to work and, if they are not able to work, through physical incapacity, then that aid should be granted to them as a pension.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one must realize in taking part in this debate, which is going into its third week, that it is going to be rather difficult to make an address without repeating what has already been said but I will try to avoid that. This evening, I do not intend to make a political speech; I think it is too early to start the election campaign. I prefer to conduct that campaign later on. I have not had much experience in election campaigns but, when they start, I like to make them hot and juicy; and I will save my ammunition for that time.
There are a few subjects on which I should like to speak, and the one that I will deal


with mainly is the amendment to the amendment, with regard to national health insurance or a national health scheme. However, there are a few other subjects I wish to touch on briefly. To begin with I want to say a little bit about trade.
We in western Canada are naturally interested in trade because we produce much more than our country can consume. Hence we are definitely interested in trade. Perhaps I might mention what has been directed as a criticism toward the government. It has to do with our loss of foreign trade, particularly with Great Britain. It may be true in part that we have lost our trade with Great Britain, but we should examine why. It is said that Great Britain finds herself short of dollars, and therefore she cannot buy our products. I do not think that is the whole story. I find that Great Britain bought more in Canada during last year than she did in 1939. It is true that during the war our trade increased considerably with Great Britain, but after the war and since 1946 and 1947 it has been dropping off. The fact remains that Great Britain spent roughly over $600 million in Canada last year as compared with $300 million in 1939. If they are spending twice as many dollars in Canada as they did before the war, I do not think it is telling the whole story to say that there is a shortage of dollars.
If they are spending twice as much money in Canada as they did before the war one might ask, and rightly so, what are they buying? Britain finds herself in a position where she believes that she needs our raw products much worse than our food, though it is true that she can use our food. But she can buy some of the products which we grow much cheaper in other countries. The Englishman has always been quite a statesman. He is the same today as he always has been, and he buys where he gets what he wants cheaper.
Take beef, cheese and butter. In western Canada we are mostly interested in beef; to some extent butter, but we do not produce cheese. What is the position? I am sure it was put on the record before by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), but I should like to cite again what the position is. In June the Canadian floor price for beef was 25 cents in Toronto or Montreal. On that same date Great Britain had a contract with New Zealand which called for beef at $14.20, f.o.b. New Zealand. Therefore it is easy to understand why we are not selling beef to Great Britain at the present time. There is only one reason, only one sensible and logical

reason, namely that we have a better market somewhere else and can receive much more for it. That is in the United States.
At the same time butter was selling in Canada at 58 cents, or at least the guaranteed floor price was 58 cents, and 35 cents in New Zealand. Last spring the guaranteed initial price of cheese was 24 cents in Ontario and 19 cents in New Zealand. Judging by these figures, if the Canadian government or the Minister of Trade and Commerce has lost these markets-and we all agree that there is a mighty good reason why we are not in them-I do not think the people in western Canada, particularly the beef growers, would look very favourably toward the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the government doing anything to force us to sell our beef and compete with New Zealand when we have a much better and higher market to the south.
We hear of trade and quite a bit about protection. I never did agree with protection. I always thought that those tariffs and subsidies were something that somebody was getting for something they did not really have. In western Canada we have to grow products and we have to compete on the markets of the world, and naturally we think that others should do the same thing.
That is all I am going to say on trade, but for a few minutes I am going to say something about freight rates. I confess immediately that I know very little about freight rates. Perhaps there are other hon. gentlemen in this house who know just as little as I do, or possibly less. My reason for mentioning freight rates is that I noticed that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has been quoted in the Regina Leader-Post of July 17 as having spoken to a C.C.F. provincial convention in Saskatoon. The Leader-Post says:
Argue says federal vote June 29, 1953
I do not know whether or not he was trying to convince that convention that he knew just when the election was going to be held.
Under the heading we find the following:
He scored the federal government on freight rates, handling of foot-and-mouth disease outbreak and floor prices.
"The railway had asked for rate increases which would permit them to operate at a surplus. Considering the government we have at Ottawa and the mentality of that government I say that they will get all they ask for," he said.
I said that I did not know much about freight rates, Mr. Speaker, but I think the statement I have quoted is far from being the fact. It is my understanding-and I am sure I shall be corrected if I am wrong, or at least I hope I shall be-that the federal
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith government has little or nothing to do with freight rates. The board of transport commissioners deals with that subject wholly. It is my understanding that in 1938 the act was amended to give the board of transport commissioners full control and full jurisdiction to decide whether or not freight rates would be increased. The provincial governments, those representing agriculture and any other bodies, may go before that board and put their case, and the board's duty is to decide whether there shall be any increase in freight rates or not.
I was speaking to a friend from my constituency who attended the convention I have just referred to; naturally he was not a supporter of mine. He asked me whether the statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia was correct; whether the federal government was going to give the railways all the increases they asked for. I asked him who told him that. He said: "Mr. Hazen Argue told us that at the C.C.F. convention." Well, the only thing I could say to him, and what I did say to him, was this: "Don't take Mr. Argue too seriously on the platform. If you get him off to the side and speak to him privately he is not a bad fellow. That has been my personal experience." That is why I mention freight rates. I am sure the hon. member will not be able to say now that I have ignored him this evening.
I have been following the hon. member since I came to this house, and I must say that generally he makes a speech that is pretty well covered up, a good defence. But in the one he made the other night he was boxing wide open, with no defence at all. I am not going to deal with that speech, but I do wish to refer to what he described as a private deal in the city of Estevan, which is in my constituency, and which he said at that time was common knowledge. Well, I have to say that I did not know anything about it. I have inquired since. I noticed that a few days later the weekly Free Press carried the story of the hon. member for Assiniboia under the heading: "Barter deal in Estevan". The Leader-Post had an article some time later, but the figures are somewhat different. The Free Press quoted the figures of the hon. member for Assiniboia, which were 100,000 bushels, as he stated in this chamber. The Leader-Post had it down to 10,000 bushels. The information I have received privately out there is to the effect that it was 8,500 bushels. Anyway, we shall take the Leader-Post and the Free Press. That is 10,000 bushels as against 100,000 bushels. Well, if my arithmetic is correct-and it is only simple arithmetic-the hon. member was 10 per cent

The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith right and 90 per cent wrong. I must admit that he is improving. I have made inquiries on the deal and I am told by the motor people that they have taken in some grain, or that at least they have agreed to take in some grain against the sale of vehicles. But in most cases the grain has remained on the farm, and must be sold through the farmer's quota book.
I am now going to turn to the amendment to the amendment, and speak for a few moments on the subject of national health insurance. I think all are agreed that a national health insurance plan is desirable. I believe we have agreed in the House of Commons that it is going to have to be paid for. I think, too, we are pretty well agreed where the money will come from, that it will be from the taxpayer.
It may be recalled that when the old age pension legislation making provision for our citizens 70 years of age and over, without a means test, was before the house, I was not 100 per cent in favour of it. I declared at that time that I had some concern in respect of the taxpayer. I pointed out that those who were receiving family allowances were riding on one end of the stick, the old age pensioner was on the other, and the man in the middle was carrying the load. I believe the people in my constituency expect me to give some consideration to the man in the middle, because he is important. If he breaks down, the other two ends of the stick will have no support and those who are riding on them will have to get off and walk.
The amendment to the amendment asks that the government bring in immediately a national health scheme. According to the figures offered by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who proposed the amendment to the amendment, it will cost somewhere between $500 million and $600 million, something more than half a billion dollars. I do not think I could justify that expenditure to the people of my constituency at this time.
Furthermore, if we accepted a scheme of this kind, it has been pointed out that we would likely find, as they did in Great Britain when they instituted their health scheme, that it would cost considerably more than was originally expected. Over there we are told it cost about $300 million more than they had anticipated. It is my opinion that if such a scheme is to be made work properly, it will be essential that those whose responsibility it is to make it work must be in favour of it. This would refer, of course, both to the people in general and to the medical men. As time goes on it would seem that professional men engaged in the practice of


medicine are beginning to agree at least to some extent that a national health scheme is necessary.
When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke in the debate he made reference to what had been said at Laval university by Dr. Jobin, chairman of the Canadian association of French-speaking physicians. He pointed out that this doctor had suggested it was time we had such a program, and that he was in favour of it. Those of us who are interested in such a program are glad to note that a medical man holds that view; but I think we will have to have more of them stating a similar view because, whether we like it or not, it is the medical men who will have to put over such a scheme, or at least who will have to help put it over if it is to be a success.
Mention has been made of our hospitalization plan in Saskatchewan, and I shall refer to it briefly. We have in our province free hospitalization available at a fee of $30 per family, as a maximum, or $10 per individual, plus a sales tax, and plus $6 million a year out of the provincial treasury. I give full credit to the part the government in Saskatchewan has played in bringing about this hospitalization scheme. I also give full credit to the premier of that province for what he did when he was minister of health to help put such a scheme across.
It has been said that one in public life in Saskatchewan dare not criticize the hospitalization scheme of that province. I take no heed of that warning. As a representative of my constituency I believe I can stand in my place in this House of Commons and point out both the good and the bad in that scheme, without suffering in any way politically.
I believe I am free to speak in that way because it is well known in my constituency where I stood in this matter before I became interested in politics. I spent a considerable amount of time and effort in putting across the hospitalization scheme in health region No. 3 of my province. That was the Weyburn-Estevan area, taking in to a large degree the constituency I now represent in the House of Commons.
On that occasion we took the municipal plans to which reference has been made in the debate, and incorporated them into an over-all plan in order to give the hospitalization service to all people in that health region. We were watched closely by the health department in Saskatchewan. The municipal representatives on the board were given assistance by the health department in Saskatchewan to make the effort a success. I

believe what was done was a success, and that other provinces throughout Canada would do well to institute a similar scheme.
Although it worked well when divided into health units, the provincial government decided to take it over and operate it on a provincial level. I have no criticism to offer on that score because I thought at that time, and I still think, that was a good idea. However, we must not lose sight of the fact that instituting a hospitalization scheme is much easier than would be a medical scheme. We had only to make deals with the various hospitals, after we had drawn a rate, and this was not too difficult. But then the medical end might be more difficult.
It has been said in the house, and I think properly so, that we in Saskatchewan are more health conscious than are the people in some of the other provinces. When the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) was speaking the other evening he said that if there was an issue in the last provincial election in Saskatchewan it was not the hospitalization plan, and indicated that all parties, including the Liberal party, were in favour of it. It is nothing new for Liberals to be in favour of social services in Saskatchewan. Indeed, any examination of the record will prove that this was the case long before we ever heard about the C.C.F.
I said a moment ago that in Saskatchewan we are health conscious, but I believe I should not leave that only as a general statement. I recall a provincial election not long ago when a hospitalization plan was an issue. I recall listening over the radio to the recent election campaign in Ontario when the Liberals promised that if they were elected they would provide free hospitalization. I heard the leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Thomson, say over the radio that that would be done, and he referred to what was being done in Saskatchewan. Seemingly the people of Ontario were not ready for such a scheme, and I do not need to tell you what happened to that party.
I think if other provinces had a hospitalization scheme such as we have in our province it would be easier to put this across. I understand that the federal government have asked the provincial governments to give their opinions of such a scheme and so far only three have reported favourably. I hope I will be excused for talking so much about my own province, but I should like to quote 68108-29
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith what Dr. Taylor, director of the Saskatchewan health planning commission, had to say about an over-all hospitalization plan. An article which appeared in the Toronto Star reads:
Dr. Taylor has suggested that this would depend on the answers to the following, among other questions:
1.	Should it be a national scheme, on the British model, or should there be ten different schemes, evolved by the provinces?
2.	Should professional associations have administrative authority? Should government funds be turned over to a profession or an association for distribution to its own members?
3.	How shall health insurance be paid for? Should it be entirely or partly financed by the state? Should it be compulsory or voluntary? Which of the three levels of government should participate and in what proportion? Should individuals pay according to a flat rate or by graded income tax levy? Should employers contribute?
4.	Should all services be provided from the start? If not, what should be included and what left out?

The Address-Mr. Cavers
I live in an industrial community. It is true that many orders from the Department of Defence Production have come to this area. They have been awarded on a competitive basis; they have been awarded to people who are able to do the job. We have a well-geared industrial capacity, aided by conscientious, experienced workers, ready, able and willing to do the job required of them. That is why they have received contracts in our area.
Contracts for over $50,000 have been awarded to such firms as Metal Craft Company of Grimsby; Canada Hair Cloth; ETF Tools Limited-; Gtenaire Limited; Grout's Limited; Guaranty Silk Dyeing and Finishing; Thompson Products; Conroy Manufacturing Company Limited; Foster Wheeler Limited; English Electric Company Limited and Newman Brothers, Limited. Other smaller transactions to local firms have been to subcontractors such as Hayes Steel Products; Court Radiator Plant Limited; McKinnon Industries Limited; Anthes-Imperial Company.
I would ask the hon. member for Eglinton who are the friends or favourites of the government in that list? Will he tell us? I would like to know, because so far as I know these people have been awarded their contracts on grounds of merit and because of their ability to do the job.
Yes, it is a fact that the county of Lincoln, which I represent, has received defence work worth approximately $11 million in the last 18 months, and much of this money remains in that county. But those contracts were awarded in a fair and businesslike manner.
I know they have provided employment for the people of that area, and I think that in fairness to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) and the officials of his department it should be made known, and made

clearly known, that one hundred cents in value has been received for every dollar spent.
I should like to associate myself with those who have spoken in the debate in favour of the appointment of a joint parliamentary committee to investigate all phases of a national system of health insurance. I do not say I am in favour of an immediate plan to provide for such a system. Many citizens are now protected by various plans such as Blue Cross, and physicians' and surgeons' services but there are others who have not been able to bring themselves within this classification.
I do not favour state medicine. It is my view that patients are entitled to have the doctor of their choice. This may not be the time to carry out such a program. As a matter of fact it is my belief that, in the light of the many heavy and necessary expenditures that must be made, such a scheme could not be embarked upon at this time. This is a problem requiring great study, one that demands the attention of members in all parts of the house. It is with that in mind I state my belief that the appointment of a committee to investigate and study the problem thoroughly would be in the interests of the country. I am sure it would be the desire of all that no one among the sick, injured or infirm should suffer through lack of medical attention or hospital treatment. I feel therefore that we should put forth our best endeavours to see that the problem is studied, and studied carefully, so that a serious and detailed report may be brought before the house.
On motion of Mr. Maclnnis the debate was adjourned.
